fixes: Replace the 'you'll know what to say' close with a real question for the comments (e.g., on the Abraham/Sarah precedent or the 'other people outside Eden' view), and cut the 'most Christians can't answer it' signpost.
Cut the 'most Christians can't answer it' filler and the 'you'll know what to say' close; end on the 'one blood' idea with a real question to the viewer.
Replace the 'you'll know what to say' closer with a real question that invites the viewer to respond, and cut the filler line after the hook.

Cut the colleague-lie analogy and use the time on the Peter vs Judas contrast, which sets up the closing question directly.
Cut the lost-job analogy. Use the time on the text's own contrast: Judas returning the silver and his remorse, set against Peter weeping and coming back.

scripts.name: Why didn't God remove the tree?
weakest: So God gave us free will, and He tells us plainly which way to choose.
So God gave us free will, and He tells us plainly which way to choose.
So God gave us free will, and He tells us plainly which way to choose.
fixes: Ground the answer in Genesis itself (what the tree was, why it stood in the middle of the garden) rather than a general free-will argument built on the steal/covet analogy.

Replace the hypothetical steal/covet argument with evidence from Genesis 2 itself (every other tree 'freely' given, the tree of life also standing there) so the answer is earned from the text, not reasoned around it.

Swap the steal/covet hypothetical for evidence from the text, such as the tree of life standing in the garden too and the guarded way back in Genesis 3:22-24, so the answer is shown rather than argued.

scripts.name: What if Adam and Eve never ate from the tree?
weakest: Work in that world would feel like tending something you love.
But death was only the first thing to change.
Work in that world would feel like tending something you love.
fixes: Swap the open-ended 'what if' for a puzzle the text can actually answer, and build the changes around that answer instead of signposted speculation ('But death was only the first thing...', 'Yet even that is not the greatest loss').

Anchor the speculation in one hard text detail (e.g. the tree of life in Genesis 3:22, the thing they actually lost access to) so there is a clear 'oh' answer instead of a mood piece capped by a C.S. Lewis quote.
Ground each 'what would be different' beat in a line from Genesis 1-3 rather than in imagination. The work-before-the-curse point and the blame point are the strongest; build the script around them.

Cut to the single strongest answer (Cornelius, stated accurately, since Acts 10:37 says he already knew of Jesus' ministry) and end with a real question instead of assuming the viewer is a Christian who was told about Jesus.
Drop the three-answers-plus-debate structure. Build the whole video on Cornelius as the single proof and land on 'how shall they hear,' so it fits one listen.

Open with the real puzzle (why would God ask Adam 'Where art thou?' if He already knew?) instead of a devotional question aimed at 'we', and cut the sermon-style lines that assume the viewer is hiding.
Open on the concrete puzzle instead of a devotional 'we' question: 'Why did God ask Adam where he was, when God already knew?' Then cut the 'you skip church' sermon lines.

Replace the familiar Exodus backstory with an actual answer: a lamb died in place of the firstborn ('when I see the blood, I will pass over you', Exodus 12:13), then connect it to Christ as the Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).
Give a real answer to 'why blood': the lamb dying in the firstborn's place, as a substitute. Cut the Egypt backstory to make room for it, because right now the payoff is circular.
